content: 1. The preferences dialog in MediaWiki allows users to customize their experience on the platform. These settings are only applicable when the user is logged in. For instance, the default administrator account is named WikiSysop. Some MediaWiki projects, like Wikia, use a unified login system where preferences apply across all associated wikis. However, on Wikimedia projects, preferences must be set individually for each wiki. 2. Users can optionally register their email address, which remains private. This enables features like password recovery and allows other users to contact them via the E-mail this user link unless the user disables this option. 3. A nickname can be set for use in signatures, which is distinct from the username. This nickname can include custom text, and if Raw signatures is enabled, users can include HTML or wiki markup in their signature. However, invalid HTML in signatures will result in error messages. 4. Images and templates used in signatures are retroactive, meaning changes to them will affect all past uses. To avoid retroactive changes, users should create unique templates or images for their signatures. Templates used in signatures must be created separately for each project if the signature is to work across multiple wikis. 5. Users should adhere to project-specific rules for signatures. Using a nickname different from the username can be confusing, and excessive or overly decorative signatures may clutter pages or draw unnecessary attention. 6. Passwords can be changed by entering the old password and confirming the new one twice. Users can enable the Remember password across sessions feature, which uses cookies to keep them logged in. However, passwords generated by MediaWiki must be changed before enabling this feature. 7. The interface language can be customized, but this may affect how certain elements, like internal links or toolbars, are displayed. For example, using English in right-to-left (RTL) language projects may cause layout issues. 8. The QuickBar, available in certain skins like Classic and Cologne Blue, provides quick access to special pages. It can be positioned on the left or right side of the page but is not available in all skins. The QuickBar must be enabled to access some features, such as renaming pages. 9. MediaWiki offers several skins, such as MonoBook, Classic, Nostalgia, and Cologne Blue, each with unique layouts and styles. For example, MonoBook adjusts the width of the left panel based on font size, while Cologne Blue uses fixed font sizes. Users can choose a skin that best suits their preferences and screen size. 10. Mathematical equations can be rendered in various formats, including PNG images, HTML, or as raw TeX code. The rendering method can be customized based on browser compatibility and user preference. Some rendering options may not display complex equations correctly. 11. Users can set limits on image sizes displayed on description pages. From version 1.5 onward, the default thumbnail width can be adjusted in preferences. 12. Date formats can be customized to display dates in different styles, such as January 15, 2001 or 15 January 2001. This setting also affects how dates appear in user signatures and other areas. However, using variable date formats in section headers can complicate linking. 13. Time zone preferences allow users to set their local time offset from UTC. This affects how timestamps are displayed on pages like Recent Changes, User Contributions, and page histories. Users must manually adjust for daylight saving time as the wiki does not automatically account for it. 14. Editing preferences include options like enabling section editing via links, double-click editing, and displaying the edit toolbar. Users can also choose to automatically add edited or created pages to their watchlist or mark edits as minor by default. 15. Recent changes settings allow users to customize the number of changes displayed, hide minor edits, and group changes by day. Enhanced recent changes provide a more organized view but may not be compatible with all browsers. 16. Search result settings let users specify the number of results per page, the amount of context shown for each result, and the namespaces searched by default. These settings help refine search results for better usability. 17. Miscellaneous settings include options like enabling hoverboxes over links, underlining links, justifying paragraphs, and auto-numbering headings. Users can also disable page caching to avoid outdated versions of pages but at the cost of longer loading times. 18. Users cannot delete their accounts or retroactively change their usernames in page histories. However, they can request a bureaucrat to rename their account. Signatures and other mentions of the old username will not be updated automatically. 19. Browsers allow users to set preferences like font size and type, which may interact with MediaWiki skins. For example, the Cologne Blue skin ignores browser font size settings, leading to potential layout issues with large fonts. 20. Users can provide their own CSS to customize the visual appearance of MediaWiki. This allows for personalized styling that overrides default settings.
